utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-PT, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. And welcome to this Pre-Trial Conference. Mr. Oric, I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand. Are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Proceed to appearances. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, together with co-counsels Patricia Sellers and Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, colleagues from the Prosecution. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with my colleague Mr. John Jones, I am representing Mr. Naser Oric in this case. We're assisted today by our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and welcome once more. I'm just having -- this is Trial Chamber III. I think my secretary has made a mess. The problem when you have a good secretary is that they file everything for you and I'm not used to that much of an organisation. Let's proceed according to an agenda which I have prepared beforehand. But before I do so, may I introduce myself and also my two colleagues. I will be presiding over this trial. My name is Carmel Agius. I come from Malta. I was elected as a permanent member of this Tribunal way back in March of 2001. I am the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II, and that involves not just this trial, but several other cases which I don't need to go into. I'm also chairman of the Rules Committee of this Tribunal and member of the bureau of this Tribunal in my capacity as Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II. Last trial I presided over was the Brdjanin case, which was decided on the 1st of September, which I'm sure you are aware of. To my right is Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt, from Denmark. Judge Brydensholt was elected as an ad litem Judge in 2001. He was educated at the University of Copenhagen and in his early years he worked at the Ministry of Justice, advancing effectively to become head of the criminal law offices in the legal drafting department of Denmark. Between 1971 and 1980, Judge Brydensholt was the director general of the Danish prison and probation service. Prior to his appointment as an ad litem Judge to this Tribunal in 2001, Judge Brydensholt served as a high court Judge in Denmark, from 1980 to 2002. It is a very considerable length of time. Judge Brydensholt has, as part of the Danish assistant to developing countries, continued to work as an advisor on the reorganisation of the judicial systems in a number of countries. I mention in particular Uganda and Mozambique. Throughout his career, Judge Brydensholt has served as either chairman or member on numerous commissions and boards, some of which are the following: He's chairman of the international study group on prison management in Strasbourg in France, and that was in 1983. On the Danish Institute of Holocaust and Genocide Studies; the Penal Reform International, a very remarkable organisation, I must say, with which I am familiar and have been familiar for the past 10 or 15 years; the Danish Society of Criminal Law, which is again one of the best societies of criminal law we have in the northern part of Europe; the Danish Helsinki Committee and the Danish chapter of Transparency International. To my left is my dear old friend Judge Albin Eser. We have known each other for quite a long number of years. Judge Eser comes from Germany, as I'm sure you are aware of. From 1954, when I was still a little boy, until 1958, when I still had not even started my university studies, Judge Eser had completed his law studies at the University of Wurzburg, Tubingen, and the Free University of Berlin, continuing in 1961 until 1964 with his judiciary preparatory service in Wurzburg. Then in 1991, Judge Eser prepared his master of comparative jurisprudence at New York University. President Meron suggests that this is the best choice that he could make, and I agree. And then in 1992 he was promoted to Doctor Luris Utriusque at the University of Wurzburg. Prior to his appointment as an ad litem Judge for the ICTY, Judge Eser held the position of director of the Max Planck, very well known and very important, Max Planck Institute for Foreign and International Criminal Law in Freiberg. Since 1982. While at the Max Planck Institute, Judge Eser was also vice-president of the German Research Foundation, and that's between 1991 and 1994, and chairman of the humanities and social sciences section of the Max Planck Society from 1994 to 1997. Between 1971 and 1988, Judge Eser was an Associate Judge of the Upper State Court in Westfalia and Stuttgart Baden-Wurttemberg, serving respectively as a member of the Fifth and Third Senate for Criminal Affairs. In 1995 and 1996, Judge Eser was a co-initiator of a committee of experts which prepared an alternative draft to the draft Statute of the -- for the International Criminal Court. In our circle we refer to it as the Syracuse-Freiberg draft, and in 1998 he participated in the negotiations on the structure of the International Criminal Court in Rome as a member of the German delegation to the UN diplomatic conference. And that's not the only place where we met, Judge Eser and myself. Judge Eser has a number of distinctions which include, amongst others, honorary degree from -- of Doctor of HC would be Honorus Causa. Doctor Honorus Causa from Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan. The university medal of Warsaw University, the honorary degree Honorus Causa from the Universidad Peruana Los Andes, from Peru; honorary member of the Hungarian Academy of Science, Budapest; and honorary member of the Japanese Society for Criminal Law; plus last but not least, he is also -- he's got an Honorus Causa doctorate from the Jagiellon University of Krakow in Poland. So I suppose I have put your mind at rest that you are in good company. And that augers well for this trial. I propose that we try and move straight to the agenda that we have. Today the understanding is that if we don't conclude today, we will continue tomorrow. But I'm sure that, with your cooperation, we should be able to conclude today. Please feel free to discuss whatever we have on the agenda as thoroughly as possible, and don't have the least concern for going into tomorrow if need be. It's not a problem with us. We are prepared for it. The important thing is that we cover as much territory as we can today so that on the 6th of October we can proceed with the case in a smooth manner, with the least possible hangovers. Now, as you are aware, we are new to this case; not just Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, but also myself. I knew I was going to be in charge of this case way back in March of this year, and I thought of preparing myself for this case way back in April or May of this year, but basically, this case was officially transferred to Trial Chamber II only a few days ago, as you are aware. Until then, it was in the charge of Trial Chamber III, which we have consulted and from whom we have had a status report before we started preparing ourselves for this trial. The purpose of the Pre-Trial Conference, and I know that, Mr. Wubben, you and your team, and you, madam, you and your team, you are fully aware of what the purpose of the Pre-Trial Conference is, but there are members in the gallery who maybe are not, and also I want to make sure that your client is made aware of this. The purpose of the Pre-Trial Conference is what is actually envisaged in Rule 73 bis (A) in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which imposes responsibility on the Trial Chamber to hold such a conference in preparation of the trial. Basically, for general information, is the purpose of a Pre-Trial Conference is to make sure that the parties are indeed ready for trial. It's a sequel to the work that the pre-trial Chamber would have carried out in preparation of the trial. This is supposed to crown it all, to take stock of the situation, and then decide whether we are in a position to proceed to trial, which I hope we are. In preparation of this Pre-Trial Conference, I gave instructions to the Senior Legal Officer of Trial Chamber II, Mr. Von Hebel, to convene a 65 ter meeting with the parties, which was convened on the 22nd of September. I discussed, of course, with Mr. Von Hebel the agenda for that meeting. I left the meeting entirely in his hands, trusting him a hundred per cent and knowing that he has done this so efficiently in the past. And of course, after the meeting I, together with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, we have had consultative meetings with Mr. Von Hebel and other members of the staff that were present. They briefed us on what took place on the proceedings in the course of the 65 ter meeting, and today we will be discussing some of the leftovers of that 65 ter conference and also other issues that he was not able to cover because of the time restrictions that he had, and also because of developments that have arisen since then, particularly in the wake of some motions that have been presented, filed by both the Prosecution and the Defence. When I say motions, I'm also including responses to motions. Well, these are pleasures yet to come. We'll deal with them as we go along. I think that, to put our priorities right, I would suggest that we start with one of the latest motions forthcoming from the Prosecution. You had prior notice of this during the 65 ter meeting. And I'm referring to the Prosecution's motion seeking leave to amend the indictment. The motion was filed last week before the end of business for that week. Briefly speaking, although I know, of course, that you are aware of what this motion is all about, but the members of the public aren't, and I don't know if your client is aware. The Prosecution is seeking leave to amend the indictment in two ways. Firstly, by seeking to remove all factual allegations pertaining to the village of Rupovo Brdo, and thus essentially remove paragraph 30 and strike off reference to Rupovo Brdo from paragraph 36 of the indictment. That's the first amendment that is being sought by the Prosecution. The second amendment, which is more of a radical one, is that they are now pleading an armed conflict, rather than an international armed conflict, throughout the entire indictment where that is applicable. Basically, this means that paragraph 20 of the indictment will now read, if the motion is granted, that: "A state of armed conflict existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina," instead of the current version of the indictment, which reads: "A state of international armed conflict and partial occupation existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The latter proposed change, according to the Prosecution motion, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond is said to be in accordance with the submissions in the Prosecution pre-trial brief. Now, I say this subject to correction, and that's because I have been out of this building from a quarter past 12.00 until about 15 minutes before we started this sitting. But as far as I know, the Defence has not yet filed a response to this Prosecution motion. Naturally, there are two options. You know that according to the Rules, you are entitled to a time limit within which to file a response. On the other hand, we have discussed, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and myself, of the various options. And we are going to tell you what our preference is. Then you can either come along or you can reserve your right to ask for a time limit within which to reply. I'll explain myself very briefly. Our desire, our wish is that when we come to the 6th of October, that is, when we come to the commencement of the trial proper, we will have this matter solved, decided. We can't force it on you. I mean, you have a right to a time limit. We have discussed it amongst ourselves and see what the implications are. We will not, of course, pronounce ourselves on what we think are the implications involved in the suggested amendments. But I would like to know whether at this point in time you are prepared to mark time and ask for time and then file a proper, formal response. In that case, we may abridge the time limit to meet our desire. Or whether you would like to stand up and say we agree, we don't agree, or whatever. In which case we can pronounce our decision here and now, to be followed by a short written decision later on, which in this case is a formality which I would recommend. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed I think it would assist the Chamber to tell you that we don't oppose the motion and we didn't intend to file a formal response. It's also our position that it wouldn't be necessary to re-arraign the accused on the new indictment because there's no substantive difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that. I think -- Mr. Jones, I think it's the way to start this trial. I fully commend it and I fully agree. There is another matter that I would raise in the wake of amending the Statute. It's a mere formality, but it's obvious that you will be charged with amending the Statute. I'd like you to refer to paragraph 5 of the indictment, and particularly in the part which reads: "On the 20th of May, 1992, members of the Srebrenica Crisis Staff" and then in brackets "(or members of the Srebrenica TO) appointed Naser Oric as the commander." Sorry. I mean the indictment as it is now reads: "On the 20th of May, 1992, members of the Crisis Staff of the TO Srebrenica appointed Naser Oric." I think it would be more correct to redraft that to read: "On the 20th of May, 1992, members of the Srebrenica Crisis Staff (or members of the Srebrenica TO) appointed Naser Oric as the commander." I'm going to leave this entirely to you. I've come to this after reading your pre-trial brief. Because in the pre-trial brief itself, the appointment of Naser Oric doesn't seem to have been reached by the Crisis Staff of the TO Srebrenica but by the Crisis Staff of the -- by the Srebrenica Crisis Staff or the members of the Srebrenica TO. I mean, this is just to tie it up with the pre-trial brief. Anyway, when we are going to hand down an oral decision now, granting your motion to amend the indictment. Please take into consideration also our recommendation. Feel free to endorse it or not to endorse it. It's something that we are not insisting upon. It is something that we are pointing out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as I hinted at earlier, the Trial Chamber, with regard to the motion filed by the Prosecution on the 23rd of September, seeking leave to amend the indictment, as explained to me earlier on, that is, firstly by removing all factual allegations pertaining to the village of Rupovo Brdo and thus remove paragraph 30 and strike off reference to Rupovo Brdo from paragraph 36 of the indictment. And third, amending the indictment by pleading an armed conflict rather than "an international armed conflict," and particularly with regard to paragraph 20 of the indictment, which should now read that "a state of armed conflict existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina" instead of the previous text, "a state of international armed conflict and partial occupation existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina," hereby grants the motion. A written version of this oral decision will be handed down, will be filed with the Registry of this Tribunal in due course. So that sorts out the first question, the first problem that we have. And in granting this motion, may I just for the record just confirm that we had discussed this eventuality amongst ourselves in Chambers, and in preparing ourselves for this eventuality, that is granting this motion orally, we had taken into consideration the requirements of Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, insofar as it requires the Trial Chamber to ensure that the charges, that the counts which remain unchanged are actually based on facts which present a prima facie basis. There is now another matter that possibly will engage us for some time. There is a motion filed by the Defence on the 10th of September, 2004, regarding Rule 68 disclosure, which has been passed on to this Trial Chamber by Trial Chamber III, as you are aware. There was a Scheduling Order that I'm sure you are aware of. Trial Chamber III decided, very rightly, that this should be a matter which should be discussed before this Trial Chamber, which was going to be seized of the case. And so now I am going to introduce this motion for discussion. On the 10th of September, 2004, basically the Defence complained that they were not entirely happy with various aspects of disclosure, but for the time being, I'm restricting the debate to Rule 68 disclosure. And in particular, they requested the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to produce a schedule of material collected in the Oric investigations and to indicate, in relation to each item, whether it considered exculpatory material or not, in accordance with Rule 68. As I said, the background to this specific, not entirely unusual, request - I explained to my colleagues this morning that I encountered such a request also in the Brdjanin case and also in some other cases - the background rests on a number of specified complaints which were in effect discussed amongst you with my Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Von Hebel, during the 65 ter meeting. Now, you were told last Wednesday, when you had the 65 ter meeting, that in the wake of the discussion, the Prosecution undertook to file a response to your motion by Friday. The response was filed late on Friday. I first want to make sure that it has been served on you, that you are fully aware of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it has, Your Honour, and we've had the opportunity to read it and are in a position to provide a reply if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. So we will -- we will proceed to my first question. I'm fully aware that the response may not cover the entire list of complaints that you had with regard to Rule 68, and I would invite you to leave out for the moment the Banja Luka collection. Please don't involve it, include it in this category of complaints. I would also like you to leave out for the time being the Vlasenica documents that you have asked, and concentrate on the rest, which is the essence of the complaints that you had in your motion of the 10th of September. In the wake of the response that has been forthcoming from the Prosecution, dated last Friday -- it's okay. In the wake of the response that has been forthcoming from Mr. Wubben and his colleagues last Friday, do you insist on your request that the Trial Chamber orders the Prosecution to produce this entire schedule of material and indicate against each item whether it is considered exculpatory or not, or do you want to be more practical, forget about this, and we try and deal with the various complaints and any other complaints that you may have as we go along?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In essence, we do maintain our motion. As to the suggested remedy of essentially a schedule being produced and a declaration by the investigator that all matters have been considered in relation to Rule 68, that was one proposal. There may be other ways of dealing with the problem. But our objection does remain and I can reply briefly as to why we maintain it, notwithstanding the Prosecution response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I can address them straight away. Vlasenica I'm going to leave until the very end, because I would first refer to the Prosecution to see what their position is. But they seem to have provided some kind of reply. When I say "some kind of reply," I don't mean to minimise or denigrate your reply, I'm just presenting myself and the position of the other two Judges as a noncommittal one. Okay. So we'll start to understand the common language as we go along, because that becomes very important. With regard to Hasanovic and Suljic, are you happy with the explanation that the Prosecution have provided in their response?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour. And if I may, the point of our motion was we provided an illustrative list of examples where we say that there had been failure to comply with Rule 68, in order to indicate what we say is systemic failure. And so to that extent, the fact that certain of these items have now been disclosed doesn't go to the heart of the issue. But if I can still take matters one by one. I can start with Dr. Hasanovic's statement. The Prosecution reply in paragraph 6 of their response, I don't know if Your Honour has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- their point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you, I've got all the documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, the Prosecution asserts that there was a 16-day period between our request and the material being disclosed. In fact, if Your Honour turns to Annex 1, which is there cited, which refers to our letter of 21st of July, it's in fact apparent from the face of that that we had already requested material in a letter of the 28th of May, 2004. And indeed, I have that letter in front of me and it does indeed refer to Dr. Hasanovic. I apologise I don't have copies, but it's apparent from the face of that letter that the delay is not 16 days but more than two months. That's just to correct that inaccuracy. The main point is that we had to request this statement of Dr. Hasanovic. That's the essence of our complaint. The statement was taken by the Prosecutor on the 6th and 7th of March, 2004. I'm going slowly for the interpreters, as I've been warned to do. That statement was taken by the OTP investigator, Mr. Nasir, B. H. Nasir. So our question is why, when the investigator took this statement in which there was a clear indication that there were documents which may have been falsified, where there was clearly exculpatory material regarding the question of command and control, why he didn't immediately upon returning to The Hague inform the trial attorney that this material existed and had to be disclosed to the Defence. That's the question which, in our submission, needs to be addressed. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond The question of prejudice isn't resolved simply by saying, well, now you have the document, so there's no prejudice. And firstly, if we hadn't asked for it, presumably we wouldn't have got it. That's a sort of prejudice. And it has been a delay of more than two months in receiving this statement. The same remarks apply to Mr. Suljic, the witness mentioned in paragraph 7 of the Prosecution response. Again, a statement was taken by the investigators on the 3rd of November, 2002, by Daniel Perry. And again, why did he not return to The Hague and say: This tends to cast doubt on Prosecution evidence and should be disclosed to the Defence? It's that systemic failure which we complain of. The main point is that these requests, or some of them, have been made pursuant to Rule 66(B). But Rule 66(B) is our initiative; Rule 68 is their duty. And we say they're not doing their job under Rule 68. And certainly if, pursuant to Rule 66(B), we ask for lots of statements, then chances are, if we're lucky, we'll get a certain amount of exculpatory material. But the chances are that we'll only ever get a percentage, because we're shooting in the dark. We don't know what they have. And that's not how the Rules are meant to function. Rule 68 means that the Prosecutor should be actively searching out this material rather than merely reacting to our requests. This is related to the issue of authentification [sic], authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we'll come to authenticity later. So try to concentrate on your complaints under Rule 68 for the time being. And particularly to what we are -- we have been made aware of, and that's Hasanovic, Suljic, Bijelanovic, Djukic, the CD on the Kravica -- attack on Kravica, and finally, Vlasenica, which is in a category of its own, which I'm sure can be handled separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm obliged, Your Honour. I didn't propose to enter into the question of authenticity in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. It's just that that's a matter which arises from their response as to when the issue became live. So I don't know if I could address that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very briefly, yes, you can, but let's not waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I will be brief, Your Honour. I do think it has to be seen in context, because the Prosecution say, at paragraph 10 of their response, that the issue of authenticity only arose at the 65 ter conference on the 28th of July, 2003. In fact, that was very early in the pre-trial stage. But if one would just turn to that Pre-Trial Conference, it's Annex 3 -- I don't know if Your Honour has that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you see the remarks there which I made on that occasion, I'll just quote very briefly. I say: "It also relates to Rule 68 disclosure of exculpatory materials. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we have the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. It's page 3571 at the top, and page 40. And I said that we wanted to ask the Prosecution to really consider seriously this issue that has come to our attention that certain documents may have been, may have been forged, and for the Prosecution to review that very carefully, and if they have any -- anything which suggests the documents indeed may not be authentic, that they disclose that to us as part of the Rule 68 disclosure. So in essence, that's a specific request for the Prosecution to pay particular regard to authenticity and to disclose to us anything which suggests the documents aren't authentic. Now, that's what I said on the 28th of July, 2003. I would say that's a very specific, emphatic request. And yet still we didn't receive these materials of Suljic until two months later, because we asked for it. Now, Your Honour, I'll move on to the other matter, the Kravica CD. The response of the Prosecution firstly was that that wasn't a breach of Rule 68. We didn't say it was in our motion. If you look at paragraph 17 of our motion, we said it was further non-disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to clear this up, particularly with regard this CD. Because you need to be on the same wavelength, and we need to be on the same wavelength with both of you. What are we talking about? Because you seem to be at cross-purposes here. I looked at the correspondence that was exchanged between you and the Prosecution regarding the disclosure of a CD. For the second time -- I need to find it here, but there was -- this CD was disclosed, according to the Prosecution, twice. And it is described in the document that accompanied the disclosure. I remember that it is Annex 16 -- Annex 17. It is described as of Serbian origin. It is described as of Serbian origin, more or less as is being maintained now in the Prosecution response, namely, they are telling you: We never really had a CD about an attack on Kravica village, but we had a Serbian -- what is allegedly a Serbian video of an attack on the village of Kravica on a particular date. So I want to know whether you are at the same wavelength, whether you're talking about the same thing or whether you're talking of two different -- because as I read you, you're expecting something different. They are expecting to have given you what they said they would be giving you in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first in terms of the distinction between a video-recording of the attack on Kravica and a Serb TV video review of a Muslim attack on Kravica, I'm not entirely sure of what the difference is between those two things. In any event, I think perhaps it isn't something we need detain the Chamber for too long, because we did have a meeting with the Prosecution on this matter. The basic misunderstanding, if it is such, is that we continue to receive a CD which doesn't have anything showing an attack on Kravica, either an attack as is described in that paragraph or a review Serb TV video review. We have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I tried to get into this and see if I could understand. Because in your response, you refer the Trial Chamber also to annex number 16. It's Annex 16 and Annex 17. Now, Annex 17 does address this event, this supposed -- the attack on Kravica. But Annex 16 apparently does not. I mean, at least from what I could read, does not really address that particular event. We have a barbecue there, we have surgical amputation of a leg, we have a few other things that have got absolutely nothing to do with the attack on Kravica. So that's why I said we need to be on the same wavelength, otherwise we won't be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it assists, in our last meeting with the Prosecution, Mr. Di Fazio was going to personally view the CD. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and if I can assist you and my learned friend, I agree with Mr. Jones that to a certain extent this issue is well on the way to resolving itself. I think the problem has arisen in that the CD contains a lot of other material other than the attack on Kravica. At our last meeting, I assured the Defence that I would go through the CD, ensure that the CD that was sent to them is precisely the same CD that we rely upon and that we claim is the exhibit. I haven't yet finished that exercise. It's unfortunately a bit longer than I thought it was to sit down and review the CD. But I respectfully suggest -- I'm pretty confident that the CD that the Prosecution has is in fact the CD that was sent to the Defence. Now, I understand from the Defence that they were concerned, because of the description in the various documents about the CD, that it might contain a lot more information about the attack, whereas in fact it has only a small amount, I understand, of information about the attack and unfortunately contains a lot of other extraneous material. So that probably, I think, gave rise to the alarm on the part of the Defence. I haven't yet finished going through the CD, but I'm confident that by the time I've finished, I'll be sure that the CD that we sent the Defence is the same as our CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if I could be of any -- of some assistance. I tried to make some sense out of this confusion, to be honest, and the best I could come up with is the following: In Annex 17 that you attached to your response to the Defence motion, this CD has got an ERN number of V000-2773. And it is described as Serb TV video review of Muslim attack on Kravica on 7 January 1993. Then there is also an indication "previously disclosed but being sent again as per Defence request of 12/12/2003." If you refer to Annex 16, which you also referred to, we have the same reference number, which is V000-2773, and here it is described in more detail. Unfortunately, none of the detail given in this description includes the attack on Kravica. It says this video consists of footage that begins with a celebration. Naser Oric is filmed for only one minute. Date on video is 2nd June 1992. Oric is in an office discussing various issues. The rest of the footage consists of a funeral, surgery of a leg amputation, and footage of men gathering for a barbecue. The time period is March to July 1994, which does not coincide with the attack on Kravica, which is 7 January 1993. So if I say I am confused, I'm being extremely moderate in my approach. I am not going to proceed any further on this. I understand, I was told way back before I started this case, that I am dealing with an excellent team from the Prosecution side, an excellent team from the Defence side. I'm going to confide myself in your hands. Please take it up. If necessary, if you require another 65 ter meeting, I will have it organised under the supervision of Mr. Von Hebel and try to sort it out. Because, as I said, reading your response, reading Annex 17 and reading Annex 16, I feel confused. I am -- and my colleagues feel confused too. I mean, we can't see any logic anywhere. So if you can deal and sort it out with Mr. Jones and whoever -- MR. DI FAZIO: As I said, if Your Honours please, following our recent meeting, I undertook to review the material and assure myself of all those matters that I mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But you understand what our preoccupation is, because -- MR. DI FAZIO: I do, Your Honours. I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I try before each sitting to go through every single page, every single paragraph, every single sentence and every single comma, and sometimes the more I do of this, the more difficult my work becomes. So -- but please try to cooperate as much as you can. The Bijelanovic and Djukic, you haven't really touched on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I can just conclude my reply on Rule 68. As I said, we gave illustrative examples of Rule 68 non-compliance. There are other examples. We know witnesses who have made exculpatory statements to the Prosecution relating to authenticity, but we won't go through that now. It will be a matter which will emerge during the trial. It will be matters which will appropriately be put in cross-examination. But we do say that we've shown enough at this stage to warrant the intervention of the Chamber to create some form of accountability, which appears to be absent at this stage. We say there has to be some remedy. For example, if the investigator were to certify Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that he's considered the statements which he's taken in the case and he's satisfied that all the Rule 68 material has been disclosed, then at least if something emerges, that investigator is accountable, as he should be, for that decision. At present, there is no accountability, we say. Thank you. If I can assist you further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. I now turn to the Prosecution. I would like -- who is going to deal with this? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would also like you -- invite you to deal with the requests relating to the Vlasenica records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this Pre-Trial Conference, I requested Mr. Di Fazio to prepare on disclosure, so he will include. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, the material relating to Vlasenica, Djukic, and Bijelanovic, has been handed over. It's been complied with, the request of the Defence, as indeed has a lot of other material that they -- was the subject of the -- of their motion. So that's the situation there. The general Prosecution response to the application --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I hesitated to rise to my feet, but my learned friend might say when that occurred, because that might create the impression that we -- it was disclosed yesterday, late last night, at 10.30. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. May I confer with my case manager to let you know when it was handed over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's important to know, obviously. And at the end of the day, if you're still not in agreement, I'm going to ask for a -- this matter can be properly addressed by -- I will come to that later, anyway. Let's not bother about that now. MR. DI FAZIO: The material was handed over last night. It consisted of a number of CDs, compact disks, together with hard copies, about two or three binders' worth. I hope that satisfies my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When we received it, because that's obviously important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Now, if I may get back to my general response to the motion: The general Prosecution response is that the relief sought is far too drastic in the circumstances, and that is clear from our response. The problem with their motion is that they advance a general allegation of some sort of systematic across-the-board failure that has been ongoing and support it with these examples. So what can the Prosecution do but respond to the specific examples provided by the Defence? And it has attempted to do so in its response to the motion of the Defence. And that's the essence of the argument of the Prosecution. The relief sought is just simply far too drastic in all the circumstances. Even if, even if the examples that they provided were clear and true examples of failure to comply with Rule 68, and the Prosecution says no. Welded into that argument, our response, is a further submission that even if, again, even if the examples that the Defence has provided were sustainable, they haven't shown any prejudice. I was looking at the submissions of my learned friend Mr. Jones, and he has failed to identify any prejudice to you. Of course, the Prosecution has set out in its response motion that it denies that there has been any inordinate delay and has genuinely and almost -- generally complied with its Rule 68 submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Di Fazio, this is not the Appeals Chamber. Let's not put together in the same basket at this stage the question of prejudice and the responsibility and obligation that the Prosecution has under Rule 68. The question of prejudice may arise at a later stage, if necessary, but at this stage, our concern, and we have discussed this thoroughly, is we take very seriously the obligation that rests with the Prosecution under Rule 68(2) in particular. And I'm sure that you -- MR. DI FAZIO: As does the Prosecution. As does the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the thing is this: I -- on one hand, I would like to make it clear, very clear, particularly to you, that we will -- we take a very serious view on this matter and that we will be very severe with you if at any time we come to the conclusion that you have fallen short of this obligation. We're making ourselves very clear on that. Because we consider it to be one of the essential cornerstones of this Tribunal and the procedure of this Tribunal. On the other hand, we are fully aware also of the immense load of documentation that you deal with in preparing cases. I fully understand that this is an exercise which takes time, which involves the exercise of one's discretion and judgement, where mistakes can happen, and genuine mistakes will be treated as they deserve, genuine mistakes. But not omissions. So at this point in time, without going much further, I think, if I read Mr. Jones' intervention well, even between the lines, I don't think it will be a case of arriving at a drastic measure that he has asked as a final remedy in his motion if the question of disclosure under Rule 68 is finalised to the satisfaction of the Defence. On the other hand, the Defence must also understand - I'm sure they understand - that this is an ongoing process, and there is no case in which Rule 68 disclosure is finalised for all intents and purposes before the trial begins. It's an ongoing process. And one has to be flexible about it. But it's an obligation that has to be met. So at this point, I think I would interrupt you -- I have already interrupted you, but I would continue interrupting you and I would suggest the following, if this is acceptable to both of you: I think since the 65 ter meeting we have already registered a significant progress, at least. Again, I mean, subject to your verifying the documents that you received last night, which I hope you are decent enough not to go through at the expense of a good rest before coming for today's Pre-Trial Conference. So I suggest that you go through the material that you have received. And I trust that if at the end of this exercise you are not happy, still not happy, if you think that there is still material that should have been disclosed, but don't be vague. Be specific. At this point in time, I can't really face seriously, look in the eyes of the Prosecution and say: Listen, have you really done your homework well? Are there any documents that you should have disclosed which you haven't disclosed? I mean, I have to work on the assumption that everyone works here with a sense of responsibility. I do not for a moment doubt the goodwill of the Prosecution, just as I don't doubt the good intentions in the objections that you have raised regarding two objections. So let's do it this way: We are going to start the trial on the 6th of October. I would suggest that you try, after you have gone through the material that you received last night, you see whether there's anything else that you would like to have been disclosed which you are aware of, not in a vacuum. I can't -- I mean, this was attempted in other cases, and the answer was always and recurrently no on the part of the Trial Chamber. I can't turn on the Prosecution and say: Madam Prosecutor, go through all the documents that you have used in preparation of the Oric case and tell me which one is exculpatory, which one is not. I'm pretty sure they haven't even finished looking at all the documents that they would like to look into. So at the end of the day, it's a question of trust. If it surfaces at any point in time that this is not being done according to the Rules, according to the law, then you don't know what will hit you, and I better not tell you what will hit you. But we will be as rough -- more rough than you can imagine. So I have full trust in you. I suggest that you try and meet amongst you between now and the beginning of the trial. If you prefer to meet formally under the chairmanship of Mr. Von Hebel, I'm sure that Mr. Von Hebel, at my request, will make himself available. You can contact Mr. Von Hebel himself if you prefer this, and we can have it arranged amongst ourselves. But I would like you to update the situation, the position, after having gone through these documents. If there are still matters relating to Rule 68 disclosure that are still not -- you're not still happy with, then I think address them in writing. We won't have any further debate on them. I will give the Prosecution an opportunity to reply and then we will decide the issue definitively, either before we start the trial or immediately after we start the trial. But this is something that has to be settled, if not before we start the trial, at the very earliest stage of the trial. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For our part, we're perfectly happy to adopt the course Your Honour suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from your part, Mr. Di Fazio, I suppose? MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I close the debate on Rule 68 disclosure except insofar as the Banja Luka basement collection is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it assists, I believe we received that also late last night. We're still verifying what we received, though I understand we've received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that has been -- MR. DI FAZIO: Handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's excellent. I come to -- I hope I will have the same answer to what I'm coming up with. Now it's Rule 66 disclosures. And as you know, there are two types of disclosures; under 66(A)(i), and under 66(A)(ii). First point: I need a clarification because I'm not understanding a hundred per cent here. Should I address one or the other? I don't know. You tell me. There was an allegation, Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, that there were some documents missing particularly from binder C. Then when I read further, I got the impression that what was really missing, correct me if I'm wrong, was only this original tape-recording or audiotape of the interview of your client by -- or from Mr. Murat Efendic. Am I right or am I wrong? Is there anything else missing apart from this original audiotape or is -- or is it just that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right, as far as the disclosure under 66(A)(ii) is concerned. However, we have to indicate that the original audiotape is missing. In binder C, which has been disclosed to us as part of the supporting material collection, we received something which should be the transcript of the conversation between our client and Mr. Murat Efendic, and we requested immediately to be given an opportunity to inspect the originals of the documents for some other reasons which are probably going to be addressed later on. And we were able to establish immediately that the original tape was missing. The original tape on the basis of which the transcript was drafted. So we were informed after that on two occasions that similar disclosure was made, and we received a similar answer as the one given in the context of Kravica. So to cut the long story short, it turned out that there is no original tape. We were referred to the series The Death of Yugoslavia as the source of the tape, and I believe that it was actually the obligation Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond of the Prosecutor to disclose to us, in accordance with the Rules, the original tape. But notwithstanding all that, I made an effort to locate the original tape to see what it was all about, to see whether the transcript was in conformity with the tape, because we only had the transcript of two men talking, a transcript which was not verified at all. And then I was -- the answer I received was that there was no such a tape. We need the tape. We need the original tape. Otherwise, the transcript should be excluded from the list of original exhibits. That is the position of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Prosecution, who is going to respond to this? Then we tackle the rest in due course. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, as I stand here, I understand that there is only a transcript in our possession, a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who made the transcript? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know as I stand here, if Your Honours please. It's a transcript of an interview conducted with the accused. Now, I understand why the Defence want that audio, any audio version, whether it be on videotape or cassette tape, to accompany that transcript. And the Prosecution will do whatever it can to locate that particular tape, because we share the same interest in getting that audiotape to the Defence, and we need it as well. But as I understand our position, we're not in possession of it. Now -- yes. If you'll just bear with me, I can let you know. We wrote to the Defence on the 18th of August, informing them that we have checked our resources and that we are not in possession of any audio recordings of the interview. 18th of August we wrote to the Defence and informed them that. We consulted our Evidence Unit in the Office of the Prosecutor. We were informed that the transcript was originally provided on floppy disk, in Word format, and it was then printed out onto the transcript and provided to the Defence. This was explained by way of letter to the Defence, clearly, on the 18th of August. That's well over a month ago that this was made clear. In an effort to assist the Defence, we informed the Defence that the interview originated from a television programme, and provided them with some hints on who to contact in order to try and get an audio version of that transcript, again, in the letter sent well over a month ago. Now, I understand the concern of the Defence. They simply have a transcript and they want to hear their client saying the words that appear on the transcript. So does the Prosecution. I can assure the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution will do whatever it can to obtain an audio copy of the interview. We have become very interested in obtaining a copy of that audio interview. But the fact remains that if we are unsuccessful in obtaining the audio version of the transcript of the interview, then it simply becomes an evidentiary issue for Your Honours to deal with at some point in the trial, if and when the Prosecution tries to produce the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you know what the consequences could be. MR. DI FAZIO: I do: I'm well alive to that. And Your Honours will also understand why the Prosecution has such a keen interest in finding an audio version of the transcript. But there's no wrongdoing on the part of the Prosecution in regards to this issue. We cannot hand over that which we do not have. And that's the problem, you see. But I raise the point, if Your Honour pleases, that this was made clear in our letter of the 18th of August, yet there is more complaint. It seems to be a case of the Defence simply not accepting what is written in black and white in our letter of the 18th of August. Now, this is my clear understanding of the situation. I can leave the Trial Chamber knowing -- sorry, with my comment on this issue, namely, that we will make every effort to locate the audio version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me ask a question. You've said in so many words that basically this interview, or the transcript of the interview, is derived from a TV programme. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm informed that that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is it -- is the entire transcript shown on this TV programme or is it the interview from which the TV programme derived some information? In other words, if we were to see the TV programme, would we have the entire interview or not? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know which is which, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Because as I understand you, is that this interview in reality happened for the purpose of this TV programme. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you have the TV programme video-recording? Madam Vidovic mentioned actually a well-known production, so -- which -- MR. DI FAZIO: We may have it, in which case, if Your Honours please, then our search is not going to take a very long time. It's not going to take a very long time. If we have it. But I rather doubt that we would have it, because there wouldn't be any need for us to be in possession of the sole diskette containing the Word transcript of the particular interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, at a later point in time, at a later stage, I'm going to ask you to bring forward -- you're aware of this anyway because Mr. Von Hebel gave you prior to notice of this, that I'm going to ask you to bring forward as your first witness someone of your choice who will confirm the provenance of each and every document that you will be tendering, seeking to tender an exhibit in evidence, with the exception maybe of those which are not contested by the Defence. I take it that if I were in your place and someone comes and tells me: This is a transcript of an interview by Murat Efendic and the accused Oric, my first question is going to be: In which language? That's number one. Second: Where did you get it from? And if he tells me this is a transcript of an audiotape, I would say: Do you have the audiotape? If he -- I certainly won't accept "I don't know" as an answer. There must be some source from which this transcript originated. So for the time being, I'm just going to tell you: Go and do some extra homework. See what you can locate. Because the consequences may not be throwing out this document automatically, but I really don't understand how you can come forward with a transcript based on something that you cannot really trace or something that you cannot show to the Defence or to the Trial Chamber. If it's part and parcel of this TV programme or of the production The Death of Yugoslavia, then bring that. I don't know. I remember The Death of Yugoslavia very well, but that was a BBC production, no? MR. DI FAZIO: It is, and in fact the letter continues, if Your Honours please. The correct title of the programme, we understand from our Evidence Unit, is: "Yugoslavia, a series for BBC 2, five parts." And we provided the name of the publisher where they might obtain the audio. And I can tell Your Honour that the Prosecution is going to approach the publisher and seek the material once again because I understand why the Defence want the audiotape, and the Prosecution also wants it. So we're ad idem on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position as I see it, Mr. Di Fazio and Madam Vidovic, as I see it, is this: I haven't seen this transcript. None of us has seen this transcript. So we really don't know what both of you are talking about. We don't know whether it's a very short transcript or whether it's a long transcript. We don't know whether really it is part of The Death of Yugoslavia film series. We don't know. But I would take it that you should -- I mean, it's no surprise that we don't know. We've just come on the case. But I take it if you have received this transcript and this has been put to you, we want to know -- we want to see the source of this transcript. Some kind of investigations have been carried out. If this transcript is a faithful transcript of what is shown in the series Death of Yugoslavia, whichever part of it it is, then we don't have a serious problem. We have The Death of Yugoslavia, then it's a question of whether we can go to that source and see whether we can go beyond that. But if it's -- it goes beyond what is shown in The Death of Yugoslavia, then that's another matter. You should be seeking at least to satisfy yourself first that what you have been given and what you have handed over to Mr. Jones and Ms. Vidovic is a faithful reproduction of the interview that was conducted, if it was conducted, between Efendic and Mr. Oric. So again, I'm going to leave this in your hands. You know how we look at it. And I think you should be able to find a solution to this without any great difficulty. MR. DI FAZIO: I think so, because we now have two teams working on it, both the Prosecution and the Defence: The Prosecution has developed a very keen interest in the audio recording and we're going to do our level best to obtain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with this, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, we are still -- we'll be having a break in about seven, eight minutes' time. Remind me, please. We're still on Rule 66(A) disclosure. I am informed that during the Rule 65 ter meeting that Mr. Von Hebel presided over, you informed Mr. Von Hebel that you have prepared a list of all witness statements, of which you have not yet received a translation, and that you requested that these translations should be made available to you as soon as possible, particularly in view of the proximity of the commencement of the trial. I would like to tackle this first and foremost. Are there still -- first of all, I haven't seen this list, to start with. That's number one. Secondly, are there still witness statements the translation of which you have not received as yet? I don't know who is going to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to deal with this. We haven't received all statements in the language of the accused. I'm referring to the statements that were taken previously in these proceedings. We had a meeting with the Prosecutor two days ago, I believe, and we agreed that these statements should be given to us as soon as possible, and the Prosecutor promised that he would invest some additional effort so that we could have the statements as soon as possible in the language that the accused understands. We provided a list of witnesses whose previous statements have not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have provided to the Prosecution, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. What's the position from your point of view? I don't know who is going to respond to this. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the Prosecution again is aware of problems with getting translations in the language of the accused to the Defence. There isn't that much that the Prosecution can do except try and get the relevant sections in the ICTY to do the translations as quickly as they can. I think Your Honours are aware of the considerable difficulties that the CLSS has in dealing with the massive workload that it faces every day. All that the Prosecution can say is that we will do whatever we can to expedite that process, that there's no benefit to us whatsoever in delaying that. On the contrary. And we're keen to do that. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond But we're hamstrung by sheer reality that exists within this institution. The whole translation problem is, as you know, a big one. If the Defence were able to, in addition to provide us with a list, perhaps prioritise within that list the material that they need the most, and we will do whatever we can to ensure that the translation of that material is done as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I beg to differ. I don't think it's the Defence that has to prioritise. I think that you have to prioritise, depending on the sequence of witnesses that you intend to follow. For example, you will probably find us creating problems for you if we come to the first witness that you intend to bring forward and we find out that his statement has not been translated. We don't mind if the last witness that you will be bringing forward in February or in March, whenever that will be, has not yet had his witness statement translated, but I think it's your problem. May I ask how many -- what's the extent of this problem? How many witness statements are we talking? Because as I take it, I mean from my experience over the past three years, when your investigators on the ground start interviewing people, most of the time they are interviewing them in the Serbian-Croat language, and the interview is translated there and then in English. So I don't understand how the translation in Serbo-Croat, which basically should be the original, is still missing. I can understand it when witnesses are English speaking only and the interview is taken in English and redacted in English, but I have a problem. I mean, I have a problem in understanding the problem in the first place. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I've heard what Your Honours have had to say on the topic and the Prosecution will ensure that all the translations are provided to the Defence, particularly the witnesses who are first called, and to ensure that the accused has all the translations of those statements in good time. But I can't -- I don't have before me a schedule of what precisely remains to be untranslated, and so I can't say to you with any precision. It would be a matter, I suggest, that I could raise with Mr. Von Hebel after this particular conference, and we can give you a more accurate list of the situation with respect to outstanding translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still don't understand, because basically what happens on the ground if Mr. X is being -- who is a native of ex-Yugoslavia, is being interviewed by an officer -- by an investigator or by an officer of the Prosecution, will be interviewed in the presence of an interpreter. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questions are put and translated and interpreted there and then to the prospective witness, to the person being interviewed. The statement is drawn up in English. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is translated into the native language by the interpreter. The witness, prospective witness, is made to sign, if he wishes or she wishes to do so, the English version. MR. DI FAZIO: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is accompanied also by a declaration of the interpreter that it has been interpreted in the native language to the witness faithfully, and it is accompanied with the text of the interview in the Serbian-Croat language. So -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't understand. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come they are missing?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may be of assistance with my own explanation. Actually, these are statements that witnesses made in previous procedures in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, or in Serbia. The Prosecutor received them, and this is in line with the Rules of the Road. But they were received by the Prosecution in the English language. I believe that that is the only way to do this. Because that's the same format that we found them in as we examined the material that the Prosecutor received in accordance with the Rules of the Road. And acting pursuant to Rule 68(B), which made it possible for us to inspect this. Perhaps there is yet another statement. I haven't seen it yet, though, one that was taken by the Prosecution only recently from a protected witness, and it can only be assumed that the Prosecutor did not have enough time to receive this statement. But the previous statements are very important to us as well, those that were given in other procedures, different procedures. But they also fall under Rule 68(2) [sic]. So I hope that we can receive this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That clarifies matters better. Anyway, again, the important thing for us, if I may say so, subject to further consultation with my colleagues, is this: That make sure that for every single witness that you intend to bring forward as we go along, any previous statements, prior statements that you should have disclosed to the Defence in the appropriate applicable languages has been done. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand there may be some problems, administrative problems. I'm fully aware of that. I mean, I encountered that problem in other cases too. And the way we have solved it, and I am going to suggest this to you, this is something that was brought up, I know, in the discussions that we have had with our staff and I understand also during the 65 ter meeting, is the question of translations. My dear friends, if you are going to insist on official translations for each and every document that we need to make use of in this Trial Chamber, we might as well forget about this case starting before another two or three years. There's no way we can have every single document officially translated and certified correct in this Tribunal. I mean, Brdjanin case I had thousands and thousands and thousands of documents, running into tens of thousands of pages. There came a time when we needed to make use of this document without further delay, and we couldn't even have the document translated unofficially, informally, inside the Tribunal. And what we did was the two parties got together, we said let's be practical, we can have it translated outside this Tribunal, so that we can proceed. And this is what I am recommending to you. Be practical. I'm not recommending send documents outside this Tribunal for translation. What I'm recommending to you is be practical. You can't expect all documents to be officially translated in good time or in real time. It's out of the question. There are other cases ongoing in this Tribunal with a lot of translations going on. We are not in competition with one another. We are trying to cooperate with one another. And so please mince my words, take it as food for thought, and I do not expect you to come back with a definitive reply here and now on this matter, but I do seek on behalf of Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt your cooperation in this matter. Please don't create obstacles on the basis of requiring documents to be officially translated, because we will get stuck and I'm sure it's not in your interests or in the interests of the Prosecution of getting stuck instead of proceeding with this case with the utmost, with the best speed possible. Okay? So, break. We will have now a 25-minute break, and there are still quite a few things, but we are moving. Thank you.

Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Vidovic. And what about the B/C/S translation of Dr. Fagel's report and, also I'm referring to 17 statements of intercepts. Have these been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know, and I look at my case manager, that the translation of Dr. Fagel's report into B/C/S has been disclosed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Wubben. And I trust you will come back later on on this. We come to something which will probably not be concluded today, which, however, we will need to deal with when we start -- when we commence the case, and that is the length of the trial. And the Defence also needs to start thinking along those lines. Obviously, the case for the Prosecution hasn't started as yet, so I don't expect you to be as categoric as the Prosecution, obviously, but we need to plan, and we need to plan for more than one reason. I mean, the Trial Chamber has got a deadline which it has imposed upon itself, possibly, to conclude this trial. We are flexible, but we also would like to have you first of all exercise some self-discipline and then we will do the rest. You had given an indication, Mr. Wubben - when I say "you," it's the Prosecution - that you required roughly 16 weeks to conclude your case. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think we can swiftly update you. I understand my colleague Ms. Richardson caused to be provided to your assistants a new --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: List of witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: -- list of witnesses. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Copies have been given to the Defence.

utterances.text: 62 witnesses -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.text: Three short of what they were before. MR. DI FAZIO: And you can see that she has gone through and listed the -- estimated, and it's always difficult to do that with a high degree of accuracy, but there's an estimate of the hours that each witness will take. So if you look at that list, the conclusion is quite simple; approximately 11 weeks, and that's just examination-in-chief. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is your position? Obviously, you don't know what these witnesses are going to say. You can only base your assessment on the witness statements that you have already. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Judging by the statements we have received, Your Honour, we are going to need a great deal of time for cross-examination, and we would like to ask the Trial Chamber to give us equal time, or as much time as possible, so that we could deal with all of it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll obviously discuss this in camera, in chambers, later on, and we will come back to you at the beginning of the trial. More or less, we'll give you an indication, but you are fully aware that we have all the authority to curtail on the time limit that will be allocated for the Prosecution and for the Defence. Anyway, there will be a measure of flexibility, of course. Much depends actually on what will be forthcoming in the course of the evidence. But we will deal with this in due course. utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might address the Court. If the Trial Chamber would like to know if there are any other types of witness motions that we'll be filing where the trial might proceed in a manner that is a bit more efficient, not having to call a witness for the entire examination-in-chief but only partially, I'd like to inform you that we are currently examining that possibility.
