utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And Your Honour, in addition to this, when the Trial Chamber comes to a point of decision-making on the procedure as such, we would like to facilitate, indeed as counsel Patricia Sellers told you, to expedite further, and then we might handle the issue of 89(F). For me it's a question of to what extent the Trial Chamber expect from us a certain or specific motion or that an announcement beforehand, which might be more practical and easier to handle than just notifying then beforehand Trial Chamber and Defence counsel that OTP would prefer and project a certain witness to be handled as 89(F) in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones or Ms. Vidovic, do you have any remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We've received the Prosecution motion regarding the 92 bis (C) witnesses, the proposed 92 bis (C) witnesses, and we do need some time to consider that motion. I'm afraid we're not in position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not something --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do note in that regard that in this witness list, James Gow is listed as expert evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. I just want to clarify for the record our understanding anyway that certainly there's going to be cross-examination of Dr. Gow. We've been discussing with the Prosecution already the length of time that might take. As for 89(F), all I can say is we're rather wary of anything which will impact on our right to cross-examine witnesses and we'll have to see that in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this matter is reserved and we'll deal with it as and when it arises. Exhibits. I have gone through the Prosecution motion, latest Prosecution motion, seeking leave to add exhibits to its exhibit list. I have also discussed with my colleagues the Defence response, which was filed yesterday. I take it that you are only objecting to five of the proposed additional exhibits, with the understanding that you are, generally speaking, objecting to the fact that what was disclosed to you is the list and not the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've since received the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. That's good. And you still insist on your objection on those five?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, this is not a matter that needs to be decided today. You are aware of the position taken by the Defence in regard to these five documents. You will have the usual opportunity that is provided by the Rules for you to respond, if you think it is necessary. And then we obviously reserve our position and we will hand down a decision later on. It could be written, it could be oral, depending on what we're doing at the time. Okay? That's -- okay. We come to the next item on the agenda that I have, and that's the opening of the trial. Opening of the trial, we'll divide it into days, let's put it like this. And on the first day of the trial, we have agreed that we will dedicate it entirely to your opening statements. Prosecution and Defence. We take it, at least this is the message that arrived to us, that more or less you require about an hour, hour and a half each at the maximum. There is even time for more if you feel -- think it is necessary. On the first day, there will be nothing else but your opening statements. I also take it - again, I asked my staff to inquire this of you - that your client will not be making a statement at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's right. That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that will be the first day of the trial. Then I'm told by -- my Senior Legal Officer has informed you of this, the system that I suggest we adopt, and the two Judges are in agreement on this, is to repeat what was done in the Brdjanin case, which was actually also then repeated in other cases. And more or less, we come from different jurisdictions. Each one of us is used to a different kind of procedure. Some of us can handle that without any difficulties. Some will encounter difficulties. I think we should approach the trial with an open book all the time. So we will be handing -- we will be spelling out to you a set of guidelines at the very beginning of the trial, these being rules that we intend to adopt and apply in the course of the trial. They are adjuncts to the Rules of Procedure and Rules of Evidence that are based on practice in this Tribunal. I can give you some hints beforehand. I mean, we will be dealing with, for example, here, evidence, we'll be dealing with the tendering of documents. We'll also be dealing with conduct generally during the sittings, conduct on the part of the staff, conduct on the part of the parties, counsel, and so on and so forth. It's not an exhaustive list of guidelines. It contains the basics that we definitely will be insisting upon and which we will be applying as we go along. And that will be handed down to you orally. I will explain the context of these guidelines during the second day of the trial. There will on that day also, we'll take up any leftovers from today and any other matters that will arise in the meantime. From my experience in this Tribunal, you can expect anything from one day to the other. So second day we will try and dispose of any pending matters that need to be dealt with and disposed of before we proceed with the trial. In particular, I am referring to any pending issues relating to protective measures, especially relating to the first witnesses, the first set of witnesses that will be forthcoming, where and if this is applicable. Then comes the question before we start with the evidence proper, there are two principal things that I would like to have done. I would have preferred Prosecution to tender all its documents as an entire, as one corpus in the beginning of the trial. I understand, and I fully appreciate, that the Prosecution would like to deal with this matter in a different manner and possibly stagger the tendering of the various documents as we go along, depending on each witness that will be forthcoming. We have discussed this amongst ourselves. Our preference is still, of course, that we try and get in the records as many documents from the Prosecution as we can at the very beginning of the trial. We understand the logic and the reasoning behind your preoccupation, and we intend to be flexible. But what you can bring forward, please do. Also because we are in the unhappy situation that, unlike, say, in domestic jurisdictions, where you have, for example, in my country, you would have committal proceedings records and you have got all the documentation there already, you know exactly what each witness has testified in the course of the committal stage, you know what the documents that are going to be made use of in the trial consist of. You have a clear picture. We start off with the disadvantage of not knowing what these documents are, unlike the Defence, who would know exactly what they are, and that creates a problem. At the same time, if we are made aware of these documents, we can have a look at them and prepare ourselves better for when they are being made use of by the various witnesses. As it happens, and as you know, if this is left on an ongoing, rolling basis, et cetera, we get witnesses coming over to give evidence, and the witness is presented with a document which is tendered as an exhibit -- in evidence, which we have never seen before. He is asked -- it may be a quite a bulky document sometimes. He is asked or she is asked questions. We are trying to follow, either in CaseMap or on hard copy or on Sanction or whatever and it may be difficult. If we know that witness so-and-so is coming over, he's going to be asked questions on what is going to become Exhibit P100 and we have that exhibit beforehand, at least we know what he is going to testify about. So it's a question of trying to meet one another's needs more than insisting on something which is crucially essential or anything of the sort. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Judge Agius, to inform you and update you, the Prosecution reconsidered their position and we will accommodate the Trial Chamber in that regard and try to tender as much as possible documents in the beginning of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And feel free not to tender them in the beginning if you require. You will help us a lot by applying this. The Defence, I'm not going to address this matter to you at this point in time, because you're not -- at this point in time, you're not required to tender any document in evidence. That will -- we'll cross that -- we come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Our concern is simply that are the exhibits to be tendered through a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm obliged. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond THE COURT: The way I would suggest that this is done, again, I do not intend to interfere with the way you would like to present your evidence, Mr. Wubben, but it's -- the desideratum of the Trial Chamber is the following. And this is what was done in Brdjanin, for example, in agreement with Ms. Korner and her staff. They were extremely cooperative, I must say. The way it was done is as such: In Brdjanin, it was divided into compartments according to regions and municipalities. Over here, I understand it's a little bit different. And you can actually stagger it also if you decide to divide your case in stages, you can stagger the production or the tendering of the documents accordingly. I don't mind that. What I would require from you is the following: That we would definitely require a list of the documents which you have already prepared, basically. You would possibly liaise with the Registrar to know beforehand the exhibit number that that document will carry once it is admitted. That's a question of liaising with the Registrar. Then I would request of you to have whoever you know is the person who is in the position to do this, but it could be an investigator, it could be an officer of the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor. The person who is in a position to come here and, under oath, solemnly declare with regard to each document being tendered, Prosecution will say: I, Your Honour, would like to tender into evidence a bundle of documents numbered P1 to P100, for example. And then the person you are going to produce, whoever that may be, will go through these documents one by one and confirm the provenance. In other words, if document P1 was obtained from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia -- of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he will say: This was handed to the Prosecution by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If document P2 was retrieved by one of your investigators during your search in Sarajevo, for example, he will testify: This was retrieved during a search made on such-and-such a date in Sarajevo by so-and-so. And, if possible, also a description of the chain of custody. What we want to make sure is that there are no doubts as to the chain of custody. In other words, if he -- for example, in Brdjanin, it was Mr. Inayat most of the time. So he recovered himself many of these documents. He could explain how these were put into boxes, shipped to The Hague, catalogued there and here, and conserved in a manner which no one could doubt then their -- the chain of custody or the authenticity thereof. So we will go through all this. For example, some may have been handled by - I don't know - AID, for example, or by the security services of Republika Srpska, for example, or from the security services in Banja Luka. You know where you obtained these documents one by one. And we will go through that. It's not as labourious an exercise as you think. We will go through all the documents in a jiffy. You will be surprised how quickly we will go through that. And then, obviously, we will reserve your position, you will be able to cross-examine the witness in due course on these questions of provenance. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's certainly one concern, that we would cross-examine the witness on each document. Your Honour did mention that this process would be designed, at least in part, to solve the question of authenticity. So naturally I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because I know very little about the problem of authenticity that has been raised, except what I read in the reports that I have received from Trial Chamber III, and also some of the motions that you filed. It's something that I am coming to now. But it's more of being a matter that will be resolved today, it's a matter that will be resolved during the trial. But I'm making it clear that we will discussed this amongst ourselves thoroughly. It's not a matter that we are going to sleep upon. This is a matter that has to be dealt with, preferably as early as possible in the trial, as we go on, but we need to know what the situation is. Obviously, I have an indication what you have been objecting to. I know that there is an expert report, but that's as far as we know. We don't know anything beyond that. So we will need to discuss that further, not today, because this is not a question that is going to be solved today. But definitely this first exercise on provenance will definitely help, because there may be documents, as we had in Brdjanin, that the provenance could not be accounted for, and there were other documents that were easily traced even to individuals, who handed them personally to whom. So at that point in time, you have a number of persons who are accountable, to start with, a number of persons that one could check with, both from the Prosecution and from the Defence, and in part, it may solve a big chunk of the problem of authenticity. But I can't guarantee you that, because I still, and none of us knows exactly what is the extent of the challenge that you have made to the majority of the documents that the Prosecution intends to bring forward. I know more or less the nature of the challenge, but not the details. You know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. In fact, the issue of authenticity, there are multiple layers to the question of authenticity. It's not a question of whether a document has been issued by the purported author or has the proper seal, but whether the information which it contains is reliable. Obviously, there are matters to be explored at trial. And I take it from what Your Honour is saying that the admission of documents at the start of the trial would almost be provisional in the sense that if it were subsequently demonstrated that a document could not be relied on, was not authentic, it would cease to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact you have actually hit the nail on the head. As I told you, we have discussed this beforehand in preparation of having to deal with this matter. We intend to proceed along the same lines as my Trial Chamber in Brdjanin proceeded in the Brdjanin case. On principle, on principle, I know that you are used to a system to which I am used when it comes to admissibility of evidence. The rules that you are used to cannot be strictly applied in the work that we deal with, especially since we are not dealing with trials that last a few days or a couple of weeks, where you can decide on the question of admissibility, plus then there is the other question of whether admissibility of documents is a matter of law or a matter of fact. It varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. And we are not sitting with a jury.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed we should say we studied the decision, the order on the sentence governing admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position will be as follows, and this is sort of pre-announcing what we will be telling you on the second day of the trial. Basically, everything that is not prima facie definitely unreliable and should not be admitted will be admitted on a provisional basis. Obviously there will be a little bit of a difference. If there is this document to which you are not objecting, then obviously that will be admitted; not provisionally, it will just be admitted. But it doesn't mean to say that we cannot go back on our decision if later on we are not convinced that that document -- so we can always revoke our previous decision contrario imperio. This is basically how we will operate. The matter, however, of authenticity, is something that we would like to dispose of as early as we can, because we will have witnesses coming to testify and they will be shown documents, and I want to make sure that the documents are -- they are being shown are not tainted documents, documents that may have been fabricated precisely to divert the course of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Indeed, as you'll be aware, there are particular concerns expressed, at least on our side, with respect to authenticity, and we've given the reasons in various pleadings for that. We're in a position today or tomorrow to elaborate on those concerns, if that would be the assistance. Otherwise, obviously, we're in Your Honour's hands as to when that matter should be dealt with and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. One other thing in relation to this: I understand that during this 65 ter meeting this was brought up and you also discussed some matters related to your desire to have your own ex parte expert to check these documents for authenticity. Of course, you will find no obstruction from the Trial Chamber. You have a right for this and we will come -- we will meet you on this. On the other hand, in your discussions, because this is what we were given to understand that you will be discussing, you will be discussing this with the Prosecution; on the other hand, while you are conducting the discussions, please keep in mind that these are originals, that if you need these originals to be transported to wherever you want to have them tested, this must not be done in a way which would impede us from proceeding with the trial. So we would have to find a way in which we can proceed with the trial, either with copies of these originals. We must also be kept fully informed of -- on how this is going to be done, to make sure that there is no way these originals can be tampered with and that these will be the originals that will be checked by your expert -- ex parte expert. But we will come to this later on. But in your discussions, the bilateral discussions that you will have, please do address all the modalities that pertain to this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I might mention one matter in that regard, Your Honour. We had a particular expert in mind which, for reasons which I won't go into but which were financial in nature, we were unable to instruct that expert. We've identified another expert, but as Your Honour might be aware, certain experts work in government ministries, for example, the expert instructed by the Prosecutor, and it's sometimes the policy of those ministries that they won't act for a private party. They require an order from the Court. So it may be that in the very near future we would need to call on the Chamber's assistance to help us appoint an expert who would then look at the documents, and hopefully, since that would be a ministry or government expert, that might also assuage some concerns about the safekeeping of the documents. But that's obviously another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You obviously understand we cannot commit ourselves to that. When the time comes that you need to do this, you'll let us know and we'll see to what extent we can involve ourselves in this, obviously. But I can't tell you here and now that we can do that. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a correction. The Dutch Forensic Institute is not a laboratory that is within the -- a government ministry in the Netherlands. It's an independent laboratory. Just to inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So basically, second day will be guidelines plus housekeeping matters, particularly related to protective measures and any pending issues. Then it's a question of exhibits and your investigator, your witness testifying on the -- on each and every one of these. You can catalogue these. In other words, this is why I said we can really go swiftly. It could well be, for example, that Exhibits number 1 to 30 were all handed to you, to the Office of the Prosecutor by Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Sarajevo police headquarters. I'm just thinking aloud. In that case, you will only need to say Exhibits 1 to 50 were handed to us by the Sarajevo police. They were received by officer so-and-so. And that's it. And he discovered 50 documents. I wouldn't imagine that if you have 180 documents each one has come from a different source. So this is why I'm telling you we can really abridge this. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the Prosecution will do what it can to accommodate the methodology that you've suggested, and I understand from your comments that initially I understood that this was an option, but I understand now that this is the definite view of the Chamber and that you wish to proceed that way, and we will accommodate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's essential, Mr. Di Fazio, because let's come down -- I mean at the end of the day, if the question of authenticity is going to be raised and even if the first stage of authenticity, say the signature, or I don't know -- we'll have to go into details. In the Brdjanin, authenticity was contested sometimes because there was no signature, sometimes because the signature was illegible, sometimes because there was no stamp, sometimes because there was no stamp and no signature, sometimes because of the source, sometimes because of 101 reasons. MR. DI FAZIO: I fully appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The moment you get Mr. Inayat, or whoever it is in this case, who says: I can confirm to the Trial Chamber that this document came from Mr. Subotic himself, handed to our officer on such-and-such a date, that is something that has become known to the Defence and they can regulate themselves accordingly. At that point in time, if they still have reason to contest that document, they will probably proceed. If, as in Brdjanin, they suddenly feel satisfied, since it has come from Mr. Subotic, for example - I'm just inventing a name - at that point in time they can withdraw the objection, and it's less work. MR. DI FAZIO: I fully understand that. I've got no problems with that and Your Honours have fully explained the system that you have in mind and I'm comfortable with that, comfortable with that. There's only just a matter -- a certain number of issues that I thought we need to raise so the matters go smoothly, and that's all I wish to do. Firstly, I understand that the Trial Chamber would be happy if the Prosecution selected a portion of its documents and handled this process at one stage or perhaps at another stage, or possibly, if it's convenient, all of the documents on that day. So the Trial Chamber will leave that matter in the Prosecution's hands, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can also do another thing, which we did in Brdjanin, and which is also -- the first batch that you are going to present here, I would say almost I would require you to have this person to go through those documents. Any further documents that you intend to tender into evidence later on, you can provide the Defence, as we go along, with a list of those documents and the source, provenance. And they would be put on notice, and then Mr. So-and-so, who will be called later on to confirm the provenance, may be required to confirm only the provenance of those documents that the Defence would like to put questions upon or would like to query. In other words, it could be another hundred documents, 80 of which the Defence is satisfied as regards provenance, and Mr. So-and-so would not be required to explain the provenance but he would be required to explain only the provenance of the remaining 20. So it's a question of liaising with the Defence. But for the first batch, please do bring an officer who can enlighten us on the provenance of the documents. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. And that immediately raises another issue, because the Prosecution can certainly bring along an officer of the Office of the Prosecution, an investigator who can give you evidence about the provenance, where a document comes from and its chain of custody here into the vaults of the Office of the Prosecutor and so on. That's not a problem. We're already working on doing that. However, this officer did not seize each and every document. Obviously many officers did, and she will be providing, I hope, evidence of various other officers and their seizures and where and when and so on. And that would be in the form of a spreadsheet. I warned the Defence because I don't want to come here on the day, introduce the officer as a witness and hear an objection from the Defence: You weren't personally involved, how can you speak about those matters? If that is going to happen, that immediately raises a problem. The Prosecution can deal with it, but we need to know now or very soon, because I can see that arising. I just raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a matter for cross-examination, depending on who the Prosecution call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is, if the officer would come here and say this I can confirm because I have consulted with Ms. or Mr. So-and-so from the Office of the Prosecution that actually retrieved this document, et cetera, what we want is someone who is responsible enough to give us the information. Now, if that information calls for further information, we'll come to that if needs be. But if we don't need to come to that, we won't come to that. It depends on the reaction of the Prosecution. But you don't need to worry about this at this juncture. I mean, just bring one officer who can at least testify on each and every document from his or her own personal knowledge, original or derived, from further investigations. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will deal with it starting from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just for the sake -- obviously we're not going to exclude the possibility that in cross-examination we'll put to the witness you didn't seize this collection yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, if the witness hasn't seized the -- that particular document or hasn't retrieved that herself, we would be required to know that. We would want to know that. But then whether we will go to the other person who actually retrieved it or not is a different matter. And the reason is that many of the persons that probably retrieved these documents are no longer in the employ of the Tribunal. This was a problem in Brdjanin. I mean, Mr. Inayat would come here and say this document was retrieved by Mr. Jones, at the time employed on the ground, employee of the Tribunal. Now we don't even know where he is. He left the employ of the Tribunal on such-and-such a day. But the reason why he would know it was Mr. Jones who retrieved document is because it was catalogued. In other words, there is a chain of records here that would lead you to the origin of each and every document. And that's what we are interested in. And then obviously we need to proceed further, we go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just so it's clear from our side - there's obviously no desire to be obstructive - it's because we have doubts about the -- some of the sources of the Prosecution documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will deal with that. So that covers more or less the beginning, the first week. Then we will deal with the authenticity, as we said, as much as we can. After that, you will begin, Prosecution, with your witnesses. I take it you are going to start with Mr. Fagel -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. The issue of authenticity of documents and evidence concerning documents is closely linked to the sequence of witnesses. We know now the Trial Chamber's desires and the sort of evidence it wishes to hear first. Do Your Honours have before you a document I prepared which contains essentially the witness sequence list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If you look at that document, you'll see that, number one, she is the person who will deal with precisely the matter you just raised, provenance. Number 2 and 3 are witnesses who deal with a very limited matter, namely, the known signatures, certain signatures of the accused. And then numbers 4 and 5 are the witnesses who will deal with their analysis of documentation in the Prosecution case, partly using the known signatures that were obtained by the other two gentlemen, 2 and 3, as you can see there. There are -- there is absolutely no problem with witness number 1, and the schedule that Your Honours envisage fits in with that and we can accommodate the Trial Chamber. I believe it was on the second day that you would like that testimony to take place, which would take us to the Friday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be the third day, starting on the third day. MR. DI FAZIO: Third day. Yes. On the Friday. Yes. On the 8th. On the 8th. That is so. We then have a problem in that our expert, Dr. Gow, is available starting on the Monday, and he -- although I understand there is a degree of flexibility that he may have during that particular week. However, at this stage, he understands that he is to start his evidence on the Monday. Number 3 on the list is now a police officer living in Australia. To get him here at that sort of notice is not necessarily that easy a task. In addition, number 4 is an expert who is currently on holidays and we haven't even had a chance to contact him, and he's back on the 1st of October. So we have some problems with getting all of these people who touch upon these subjects here at the one time and flowing in their evidence one after the other, in addition to which we have, of course, the problem that Dr. Gow, we very much hoped to put him on at the beginning and he also has his personal commitments and that would inevitable cut into the smooth and orderly sequence. So we can accommodate the Trial Chamber to a large extent, but we do have some of these problems and we ask for the Trial Chamber's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You certainly, I can assure you, you will not encounter difficulties, Mr. Di Fazio. I mean, we understand that these problems will occur as we go along, and you will -- provided that they are not self-inflicted, we will cooperate. There's no question about that. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it may be that the Defence might be minded, for example, to consent to the evidence of Keli [phoen] and Teda [phoen], numbers 2 and 3, going in. Their evidence is very limited. Essentially, I saw the accused write, here are the documents, here is his signature, here are the documents that he wrote on. That's the nature of it and that's as far as it goes. I don't know if they're minded to agree to that or not. But in any event, that's the problem. So could I suggest to the Trial Chamber that we do call number 1 on the day that you suggested and she will be the person who gives evidence about the provenance of the documents. Then call our expert, Dr. Gow, and then as soon as we can thereafter, as soon as we can thereafter, call the -- all the other people who touch upon the issues of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, that's your problem. We will not tell you how to proceed, which witness to bring first, which witness to bring second. That's not our job. That's up to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I suggest is that you have chit-chat with the Defence on that and then what we require only is that you keep us informed. That's all. Because we too have to prepare ourselves. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. Your Honours, may I just say, in my Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond comments we're saying this: This is essentially the basic sequence of witnesses that the Prosecution wants to present. We will do our level best to get witnesses who talk about documentation here as soon as we can, early in the trial, but we ask that the Trial Chamber bear with us at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. This brings me to an issue that I know was raised during the 65 ter meeting on which I will dwell very shortly. Each of these witnesses, with the exception of the experts, et cetera, would have given statements to the Prosecution in the course of the years that preceded this trial. Now, I come from a jurisdiction where we would hear the evidence of the witness and we would not have at our disposal any witness statement made prior to the trial. As I said, that makes sense, first of all, where it is the rule, as it is in my country. And it makes sense also where you have a procedure, a system in place which would ensure in any case that when the case comes to trial, the Presiding Judge, with or without a jury, would have at least the committal proceedings at his disposal. Over here, you get a list like this showing Miladin Sic [phoen] giving evidence. It's true, we also have very short, succinct summary of what supposedly this gentleman is supposed to testify upon. But we come here and basically we are the last -- the least persons to know what this gentleman is going to testify about. This is a matter that has been discussed at length amongst us Judges, the permanent Judges and the ad litem Judges of this Tribunal over the time, and the approach is that there is no hard and fast rule that should be adopted. There are a lot of advantages that can be gained by the trial Judges if they have at their disposal, not in the beginning, but as we go along, staggered, okay, week after week, a copy of the witness statements, for various reasons. First of all, certainly not because we want to influence ourselves negatively. We are three expert, experienced Judges, I mean, so we are not a jury. We are -- in other words, the reason why we require these to be made available is that we know beforehand what the witness is going to testify about, what he stated to the offices of the Prosecution, and then as we go along, we can actually make a better assessment of where we are and we would know also if it's the case of us putting some questions or not. In many cases, basing myself on my past experience, you end up having to look at these witness statements in any case, because sometimes it's the Prosecution that would refer the witness to the previous witness statement, sometimes it's the Defence that will refer him. So the position taken is the following: That I discussed this with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser. I explained to them what the position is in this Tribunal. I told them what my preference is, even though I come from a jurisdiction when this is not done, I still see a lot of benefits in it in this Tribunal. And I told them that they are free to decide individually, on an individual basis. It's not something that I can put in place or ... And the decision is that each one of us requires them to be handed to us on a regular basis, on a weekly basis. Now, whether we will all read them or whether only some of us will read them, that is a question that we will decide amongst ourselves. It may well be that one of us or more than one of us will not read them. But it's a question of we need to have them at our disposal, not in one bulk, as I said, please, because that would create problems. If next week it's Mr. Zivanovic who is going to come and give evidence, let us have a copy of his witness statements, if there are any, the week before. Also sometimes it happens - and I need to make myself clear - sometimes -- not sometimes. The Prosecution usually brings these witnesses a few days before they are about to testify, and they are briefed and sometimes they release new statements. On many occasions, you get new witness statements a day or two before they come here to give evidence. In that case, I would like the Prosecution to do its utmost to disclose them to the Defence as early as you can. I know that sometimes it's -- there is very little time. Many a time this is done over a weekend. I am aware of that. But I appeal for your cooperation, the utmost that you can do, please, because sometimes they will be taken by surprise, come here and know that witness so-and-so has actually released another statement 24 hours before coming here to give evidence. So these are problems that I would like you to be very transparent in your interrelationship, okay? CaseMap. CaseMap. Yes. We are very happy to cooperate with you, whether it's CaseMap or whether it's Sanction. Please feel free to make the best use of these two systems. What I would like to ask you is if you could kindly both, the Prosecution and Defence, if you have all your documents already compiled, as you obviously have, whether you could furnish on CD-ROM to our staff a copy of the documents beforehand, so that we will be in a position to make the best use we can in the course of the trial. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we actually have our documents that organised electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, but once you have them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What we could certainly do is when we present a document or an exhibit to a witness, provide an electronic copy simultaneously, but we certainly haven't even formed a view as to which documents we're going to be using. We'll certainly do it as the court progresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One of our staff will liaise with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is this: Again, you should take it as a guideline from now, that when you are filing a document into -- you're tendering it into evidence, please make sure that you provide us with a hard copy and also with an electronic copy. When I say provide us, not directly to Judge Eser or Judge Brydensholt and myself. I mean, you know the procedure. But please try to ensure that we are provided also with an electronic copy of it, okay? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just one issue that arises from the point that Mr. Jones raised. I take it from his comment that there's a possibility that documents will be produced I assume during the course of cross-examination to Prosecution witnesses. Does the Trial Chamber have any view as to when the Prosecution might receive those documents; as and when they're produced to the witness in the box or beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're rather in Your Honour's hands as far as that's concerned. It's also a matter which we'll be reviewing during the course of examination-in-chief which documents to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The problems that I envisage only relate to the fact that you brief your witnesses before you bring them over. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what you say about -- no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Briefing. But in the sense that if -- I would -- in the normality of cases, I would ask the Defence to disclose to you documents which they intend to make use of in relation to a particular witness. On the other hand, I mean I don't want to involve the Trial Chamber too much in that, because, as I said, I mean, a system is in place here which is normally not in place in national jurisdictions. I don't know, but let's play it by the ear and we see how we go along. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be in many cases that the documents we would be using are already in the Prosecution's possession. If we were to provide all the documents which we think we might use before we cross-examine a witness to the Prosecution, it could rather radically change the whole nature of the adversarial proceedings. They would anticipate those documents being used and would deal with them beforehand and it would be impossible for us to plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the whole purpose of disclosure. But the thing is you do not have a legal obligation to disclose, while the Prosecution does. So this is -- one has to balance ... I'm afraid to get the Trial Chamber involved in this beyond what I have said, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because of the system that we have in place, you know. I mean, it's ... I won't say more than that. But there are -- yes. The pre-trial brief of the Defence. Now, let me find it. Yes. Could I refer you -- these are matters that were not raised in the 65 ter meeting because of time constraints. Mr. Wubben, do you have the Defence pre-trial brief handy? Okay. Can I take you to paragraph 25, please. We are not going to deal with these issues now. I'm going to ask you -- you may sit down, actually, Mr. Wubben, because you're not going to be asked to give an explanation today. I'm just pointing out the following paragraphs which you can read later on. And we will give you, say, two weeks from now to possibly address these problems that have been raised by the Defence. In paragraph 25 of the Defence pre-trial brief, they refer you to your paragraph 38 of the Prosecution brief and suggest that there is no source for the proposition set out in your -- so please go through that, because the Defence is not accepting it and we would like to know what your position is in regard. That's number one. The second is in paragraph 34. Here the Defence raises the following matter: They refer to a part of your pre-trial brief in which you quote, mention, quote Bosnian Serb women and children. The Defence submits that no crimes against Bosnian Serb women and children are charged in the indictment against their client. Anyway, they make a submission. Please look into this matter in the two weeks that you will be given, try to come back with an explanation or with some kind of remark. Next is contained in paragraph 59 of the Defence pre-trial brief. Again, this is self-explanatory. I needn't go into details now because it will take me another five minutes. It's paragraph 59. Please try to address it in your response. Then it's paragraph 65. Again, your attention is being drawn to the Defence position, something that they allege that should not be in the indictment and should be struck off from the Prosecution brief. I don't know how much -- how important it is to have it struck off from the Prosecution brief. It doesn't bind the Trial Chamber. But in any case, please go into that and come back with a response. And the next paragraph is paragraph 66, which is immediately following. Again, those are the five paragraphs that call for some kind of a response from the Prosecution, in our opinion. We are giving you two weeks. We think it's sufficient. If it's not sufficient, we'll obviously extend the time, as required. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was raising prior to your remarks in this regard because, with a view to those five issues, I prepared orally a submission and clarification. That will take us about eight, ten minutes. So I took the time to perhaps to enable you to address other issues, because I noticed that the Senior Legal Officer at the 65 ter conference indeed stipulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you have them reduced in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will spare us. I mean, it's not a big job, I think. If you have the notes already, you can easily have them translated into a proper format.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. I will make a written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, are there any other issues that you would like or matters you would like to raise? Because we are soon coming to an end. Are there any other matters that you would like to raise? Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise. There is this matter of the English versions of the intercepts statements you referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I contacted my case manager and she confirmed to me that it should be disclosed, we should be able to disclose it by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very good. That's very good. Now, before we come to the end, let me make it clear that I have tried, in consultation with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and our precious staff and our secretaries, to put together all the issues that we thought needed to be dealt with during today's Pre-Trial Conference. I am aware that we haven't covered everything. We've covered most things, I think, but there will be other things that will come to your mind, to our mind, and to the Prosecution's mind. This is not the end of the story. If there are any leftovers or other things that you need to discuss, we can either have an additional hearing, which will be a continuation of today's Pre-Trial Conference, before we commence the trial, or we can have them raised and discussed, debated, the first days of the trial. In other words, I'm leaving all these options open. But if you think that there are serious matters to be discussed before the trial commences, then you will find us available, we will hold another Pre-Trial Conference in addition to that of today. Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a very short question to put to you, but to us, I can assure you, is of extreme importance. We want to make sure that you do not have any problems with regard to your condition of detention, that, in other words, you're being treated well in the Detention Unit. And we also want to make sure that you do not have any health problems that we should be made aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no problems whatsoever. Everything is fine. Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If any problems do arise, your channel of communication is through your lawyers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, this being so, I think my duty is to thank each and every one of you. You've been extremely cooperative, I must say. It's what also we expected. We can adjourn today. We've managed to conclude the Pre-Trial Conference in one sitting and even before the allocated time. I thank you all, and please God, we will reconvene on the 6th of October and start, commence the trial. I thank you. My legal officer will be approaching you now also.
